cues.say: Component thirteen: the waiting room.
A waiting room is a holding page that sits in front of your site. When demand is too high, visitors wait there in line, and they're let into the real site at a fixed rate.
You don't build it. You switch it on at your CDN, or buy it from a vendor like Queue-it.
Why do you need one? Picture a sale that starts at an exact minute. Thousands of people sit on the page, pressing refresh.
At the start, they all hit the servers in the same second, and the site falls over for everyone.
And even if it survives, it isn't fair. Whoever has the fastest connection, or a bot, gets in first.
So instead, every visitor lands on the line page first, and gets a place in line.
Everyone who arrived before the start is shuffled, so being early, or fast, doesn't put you first.
Then the waiting room lets people in at a fixed rate, the rate your site was load tested for. Everyone else watches their place count down.
Each person let in gets a pass, stored in a cookie, so they can move around the site without queueing again.
When do you use one? First, when demand is far above what you can serve, even after adding servers.
Second, when a sale starts at an exact minute, and everyone arrives at once.
Now a real case. An electronics shop's sale starts at exactly six AM. Forty thousand people are refreshing, and checkout was tested for three hundred a second.
Without a waiting room, forty thousand requests land at once, and checkout falls over at six o'clock.
With one, it lets in three hundred a second, so checkout runs at the load it was tested for. The last person in line gets in a little after six oh two.
It sits at the edge, in front of everything, often as a CDN feature. Visitors with a pass go straight through.
On a normal day it's off, behind a feature flag: a switch you flip without deploying code.
Two trade-offs. Waiting is a real cost to your customers, so only turn it on when traffic beats the plan.
And the rate is only as good as your load test. Let in more than you tested, and the site falls over anyway.
In the interview, say: the waiting room is behind a flag, on only if traffic beats the plan.
